h1: Beer with sushi and Japanese food beyond rice lager
title: Beer with Sushi and Japanese Food | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer pairings for sushi, sashimi, tempura, ramen, yakitori and karaage, beyond the usual rice lager, with styles that suit umami and delicacy.
teaser: A crisp rice lager is the default with sushi. It is not the only good choice, or always the best.
standfirst: Japanese food is delicate, savoury and built on umami. The usual pairing is a pale rice lager, which works for a reason. Here is why it works, plus what else is worth trying when you want more flavour.
sections: Why rice lager became the default

Japanese mainstream lagers often use rice alongside malted barley. Rice adds fermentable sugar but very little flavour or colour, so the beer comes out pale, light bodied and dry. Our guide to tasting rice and maize in lager explains what adjuncts do to flavour.

That dry, clean profile is a good match for delicate food. It refreshes without covering subtle flavours. So the rice lager is not a bad choice with sushi. It is a safe one. The question is whether other beers can add something without overpowering raw fish.

Sashimi is raw fish, sliced and served with soy sauce and wasabi. Nigiri puts it on hand pressed rice seasoned with vinegar, sugar and salt. The flavours are subtle: clean fish, gentle sweetness and the umami of soy.

Anything big and bitter will flatten this. A German Pilsner at 4.5 to 5% ABV is a step up from rice lager: still crisp, but with floral hops and a little more malt. A Kölsch is even softer, with a faint fruity note. With fatty fish such as salmon or tuna belly, the extra bitterness of a Pilsner helps cut the oil.
Wasabi, ginger and soy change the beer

Wasabi is pungent rather than hot in the chilli sense. It hits the nose and fades quickly. Pickled ginger (gari) is sweet, sour and sharp, meant to clean the palate between pieces. Soy sauce is salty and savoury.

Salt and umami make beer taste less bitter and fuller, which is why soy and Pilsner work so well. Pickled ginger can make a very hoppy beer taste odd, so keep the hop aroma restrained. A Belgian witbier is a good bridge here, its coriander and citrus sitting comfortably beside ginger and rice vinegar.

Tempura is seafood and vegetables in a light, crisp batter. Karaage is Japanese fried chicken marinated in soy, ginger and garlic. These are the fried dishes on the menu. Fried food is where beer is strongest.

A Pilsner or a crisp lager is the natural match, its carbonation of around 2.5 volumes scrubbing the oil away. A saison, dry and highly carbonated with a peppery yeast character, adds more interest. With karaage and a squeeze of lemon, a pale ale at 30 to 40 IBU is also good.
Ramen, yakitori and the rich dishes

Ramen is a bowl of wheat noodles in a rich broth: tonkotsu (pork bone), shoyu (soy), miso or shio (salt). Tonkotsu in particular is creamy and full of fat. Yakitori, grilled skewers often glazed with tare (a sweet soy glaze), brings char and caramel.

These can take darker beers. With tonkotsu or miso ramen, a dunkel or a schwarzbier brings toasty or lightly roasted malt without too much body. With tare glazed yakitori, an amber lager or a brown ale matches the caramelised glaze. Unagi, grilled eel with a sweet glaze, is lovely with a schwarzbier.
Sake is not the only Japanese match

Sake is a great partner for Japanese food. Many restaurants in Indian cities now list it. It is brewed from polished rice with koji mould and yeast and is usually 14 to 16% ABV, so it is a very different drink from beer. Beer offers carbonation and bitterness, which sake does not. Those two help most with fried and fatty dishes.

If you are building a Japanese meal at home, there is no rule that says you must pick one. Many people enjoy beer with the fried courses and something else with sashimi. Our beer and food pairing basics cover the general principles.

Japanese food in Indian cities also comes with local twists: spicy mayo rolls, cream cheese rolls and tempura rolls with sriracha. These are richer and hotter than traditional sushi. A cream cheese roll wants the carbonation of a Pilsner. A spicy roll with chilli mayo is happier with a witbier or a hefeweizen, whose low bitterness keeps the heat in check.

Try this simple test. Sip a Pilsner and note how bitter it feels. Then dip a piece of sushi in soy sauce, eat it and sip again. Most people find the beer tastes rounder and less bitter after the soy. That is salt and umami softening bitterness. It is also why savoury Japanese food handles more hops than its delicacy suggests. Serve lagers at 4 to 6 °C for sushi, since warmer beer can taste heavy next to raw fish.

Your first step: next time you order sushi, ask for a Pilsner or a Kölsch alongside the usual lager. Taste them with the same piece of salmon nigiri and see which one you prefer.
faqs: What beer goes best with sushi?
A crisp German Pilsner or Kölsch is a step up from rice lager, adding a little hop and malt character without overpowering raw fish.
A dunkel or schwarzbier. Their toasty or lightly roasted malt suits the rich pork broth without feeling heavy.
Why does soy sauce make beer taste less bitter?
Salt and umami suppress the perception of bitterness, so beer tastes rounder and fuller after savoury food.
